B1 · Listen and answer · at this level
What day is the deadline for the new numbers?
“The deadline is on Friday. The supplier want the new prices by Friday, but the speaker is not sure they can make it.”
You got the main point: the deadline is Friday and the speaker is unsure. Remember the -s ending for one supplier: it wants, not want.
B2 · Say it · not yet
Your American director asks: do you think it's better to finish a project early with less detail, or take longer and get everything right? Give your opinion and say why.
“In my opinion it depends on the project, but generally I prefer to take longer and get everything right. When we deliver a product with quality issue, the cost for fix it later is much more higher than one week delay. Of course the stakeholders want the deadline, so I try to make a compromise, for example we deliver the main functions early and the details after. But I don't like to do a mistake what customer will see.”
Clear opinion and good reasons. The thing holding English back is double comparatives: say 'much higher', not 'much more higher'.
B1 · Say it · at this level
Your American director wants to talk about a project. Tell him about one deadline you had at work that was hard to meet. Say what happened and why it was difficult. Use two or three sentences.
“Last year we had a very hard deadline for launch of new product. The supplier delivered the parts two weeks late because they had a quality issue, and we was under big pressure from stakeholders. It was difficult because we must do the testing again and in the same time keep the original date, so my team worked many weekends.”
You explained the deadline and the problem clearly, using because and so. Watch 'we was' (we were) and small words like 'the'.
B2 · Say it · not yet
Your American director asks: is it better to deliver a supplier order on time with a few gaps, or wait a week and get everything complete? Give your opinion and one reason.
“In my opinion it is better to wait one week and deliver everything complete. The reason is that when we deliver with gaps, the customer must make a lot of additional communication and the cost of fix it later is more higher than one week delay.”
Your opinion and reason came through clearly. What held the English back was the double comparative: say 'more expensive', not 'more higher'.

judge.voice: Fine, B1, not C1. I'll grudgingly accept it, because it quoted my own sentences and the supplier-deadline tasks were my actual job. That's not baby stuff. But the feedback was thin. It caught 'much more higher' and 'we was', yet said nothing about 'discuss about' or 'do a mistake', which my new director would notice. And 'say more expensive'? That's not what I meant; higher is the word. One wrong fix and I start doubting the rest. It took far less than a language-school placement test, so the time was worth it. I'd come back if the practice targets my real recurring errors. I'd tell colleagues it's quick and fair on level, but not yet a proper diagnosis.

findings.title: Scene fits job, pitch holds, moment correct
findings.got: Workplace supplier scene at B1. The partner kept pace and the single moment was accurate, with a short reason.
findings.evidence: #2 Priya "What options would help you most?"; #4 "A plural noun needs a plural determiner"

judge.voice: Good scene, finally something real: a supplier, a delay, a deadline. Priya spoke at a sensible level, no baby talk, and the date got agreed. The one correction, "these parts", was right and short. But look, I said "discuss about", "reason of", "until Wednesday" and "since two weeks", and nothing. The recap showed one fix and a random phrase, "much higher". If this is meant to fix what makes me sound junior to the new director, it missed the things I actually do every week. I would not trust it to find my real errors yet. The scene was worth the time, the feedback was not. I'd try one more time before telling anyone.

prior.evidence: #5 "discuss about", "until next Wednesday" and #6 "since two weeks" drew no moment. Only turn 1 got one; #8 "1 moment to keep".

verdictWhy.text: C3 failed: #3-4 only moment is "waiting for this parts" → "these parts", not one of his listed fossilised errors. "discuss about" (#5) and "since two weeks" (#6) drew nothing.
